o1.biggest_strength: It uses our data well: it spots that comparison pages drive trials, not blog traffic, and gives the team a concrete month-by-month plan plus a real first-week task list.
o1.biggest_mistake: The priorities slip in places: a docs CTA projected at +25 trials is ranked below a cookie-banner rewrite projected at +3, and the high-intent cookie/cookieless pages are not both tackled immediately. It also has at least one risky factual claim about competitors' hosted/self-hosted options.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Move the cookie-banner and cookieless analytics rewrites into week one or month one, fix the competitor fact issue, rank dev tasks by trial impact, and cut or justify the unproven new agency/import pages with search demand.

o2.biggest_strength: It is tightly tied to trials, not traffic, with sensible math, conservative projections, ready-to-use titles, and clear day-60/day-90 rules the team can act on.
o2.biggest_mistake: It is a little too hands-off with pages that already win, especially docs; I would still use high-ranking docs like WordPress to send more qualified visitors to trial. The cookie-banner rewrite could also come sooner.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add internal trial links from the strongest docs pages, bring the cookie-banner page into month one if capacity allows, and make the month-two comparison refresh list explicit so it cannot accidentally include pages we meant to leave alone.

reason: I would rather hand Output 2 to the team because it is more disciplined, more realistic about trial gains, and closer to publishable as an operating plan. Output 1 is strong, but it needs more cleanup around priorities and a factual competitor claim before I would use it.
